cards.subtopic: The patient who wants to leave against advice
cards.question: RMO case: The patient who wants to leave against advice — what is your immediate management approach?
cards.answer:
FIRST: Sit down and find out why. Do not treat it as a confrontation.

THEN:
1. Common reasons: pain, fear, boredom, carer responsibilities, pets, cost, withdrawal, feeling unheard, family or cultural obligations.
2. Assess capacity for this specific decision. If they have capacity, they may leave.
3. Explain the risks in plain language, use an interpreter if needed, document the discussion, and offer the best available alternative — a partial plan, early follow-up, oral instead of IV antibiotics, a clear return plan.
4. Give them a discharge summary and medications, and make it clear they are welcome back.
5. If capacity is impaired, or there is a mental health or safety concern: escalate to your registrar and consultant, and consider the Mental Health Act or guardianship. Do not resolve this alone.
6. “Patient is hypotensive.” Go and see them. A to E, fluid challenge, work through the four types of shock, check the drug chart for antihypertensives and opioids, escalate.
7. “Patient is tachycardic.” ECG first. Then sepsis, hypovolaemia, pain, PE, arrhythmia, withdrawal, thyroid, anaemia.
8. “Patient is febrile.” Septic screen and examine for the source: chest, urine, skin, line, wound, abdomen, CNS. Cultures before antibiotics unless unstable.
9. “Patient is hypoxic.” Oxygen to target, sit up, gas, CXR, ECG. Pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, PE, pneumothorax, atelectasis, aspiration, mucus plug.
10. “Patient is confused.” Delirium screen, sugar, hypoxia, sepsis, pain, retention, constipation, drugs, withdrawal. Collateral history for the baseline.
11. “Patient hasn’t passed urine.” Bladder scan first. Retention, or AKI, or a blocked catheter.
12. “Potassium is 6.5.” ECG now, monitor, stabilise–shift–remove, then go through the drug chart.
13. “Sodium is 118.” Symptomatic? Volume status? Correct no faster than 8–10 mmol/L in 24 hours.
14. “INR is 8.” Bleeding or not? Withhold, vitamin K, PCC if bleeding. Find the interacting drug.
15. “BGL is 2.1.” Treat now, recheck in 15 minutes, then find out why. Sulfonylurea means admission.
16. “Patient has chest pain.” ECG within 10 minutes, and compare it with the old one.
17. “Patient fell.” Assess before moving them. GCS, anticoagulation, CT if head strike on an anticoagulant, find the cause, incident report, tell the family.
18. “They pulled out their NG tube or cannula.” Ask whether it is still needed before replacing it. Consider delirium as the reason.
19. “Patient is in pain.” Assess it properly, use the analgesic ladder, treat the cause, and think about constipation and retention. Prescribe an aperient with every opioid.
20. “Patient is constipated.” Examine the abdomen, exclude obstruction and impaction, review opioids and anticholinergics, mobilise, hydrate, softener plus stimulant.
21. “Patient is vomiting.” Antiemetic chosen for the cause, exclude obstruction and raised intracranial pressure, check electrolytes, review drugs. No metoclopramide in Parkinson’s or bowel obstruction.
22. “The IV site is red.” Remove the cannula. Phlebitis, cellulitis or extravasation? Document, re-site elsewhere, and ask whether they still need IV access.
23. “Please chart some fluids.” Assess volume status first, choose the fluid deliberately, add maintenance plus deficit plus ongoing losses, check the UEC, and never chart potassium blindly.
24. “Please certify this death.” Confirm death formally, document the examination and time, complete the certificate honestly, consider whether it is reportable to the Coroner, notify family and GP, and check donation and cultural requirements.
25. “Can you consent this patient?” Only for a procedure you understand and are credentialed to explain. Otherwise the proceduralist consents. Capacity, information, voluntariness, documentation, interpreter if needed. Part D — ED questions that are not cases “How do you prioritise when the waiting room is full?” • Triage category sets the order, but I’d re-triage actively — someone waiting two hours may have deteriorated. • The nurse in charge is my source of truth about who has changed. • Quick reviews to spot the sick early, start investigations at triage where protocols allow, and be honest with people about waits. • And I’d tell the ED consultant when the department is beyond what is safe. “A patient wants to leave the waiting room before being seen.” • Try to see them briefly, or at least get a set of obs. • Explain the specific risk, not a general one. Document it. • Offer an alternative such as GP review, and give clear return advice. • Escalate if I had any concern about capacity or serious pathology. “How do you hand over in ED?” • ISBAR, at the bedside where possible. • What has been done, what is pending and who is chasing it, the plan, and the disposition decision. • Pending results are the highest-risk item, so I name them explicitly. “What does the Australasian Triage Scale mean to you?” • It sets the maximum time to clinical assessment by acuity — category 1 immediate through to category 5 within 120 minutes. • It tells me the order to work in, but it is a starting point, not a diagnosis. • Patients get re-triaged when they change. “You disagree with a senior’s disposition decision.” • State my concern clearly and give my reasoning once, and ask what I’ve missed. • Accept the decision if it stands — but document my assessment factually and hand the concern over explicitly. • If I genuinely believed the patient was at risk of serious harm, I’d escalate to the ED consultant. • Disagreeing respectfully and escalating are both part of the job. “The patient needs admission but there is no bed.” • Keep managing them as an inpatient in ED — the care does not pause because the bed hasn’t appeared. • Ongoing obs, regular review, medications charted and given on time, VTE prophylaxis, pressure areas, food and fluids if appropriate. • A clear owner for the patient. • And escalate access block to the ED consultant and bed manager, because it is a system problem. Part E — General Medicine questions that are not cases “What makes a good general medical RMO?” • Someone who does the unglamorous things reliably: an accurate medication chart, a discharge summary written on the day, results chased and acted on, families updated, problems escalated early. • These patients are complex and elderly, and most harm comes from omission rather than error — so thoroughness is the skill. “How do you run a ward round efficiently?” • Prepare first: obs, results, overnight events, and what yesterday’s plan was. • Document as you go, with a clear problem list and a dated, actionable plan. • Afterwards prioritise jobs by urgency, delegate what can be delegated, and tell the nursing staff the plan rather than assuming they read the notes. “How do you approach a patient with multiple comorbidities?” • A problem list, not a single diagnosis. Rank the problems by what is driving the admission. • Be explicit about how treating one affects another — diuresing a heart failure patient with renal impairment is the classic. • Involve the relevant teams but keep ownership of the whole patient. • And anchor it in what the patient actually wants, especially where there are trade-offs. “Why do patients get readmitted?” • Usually medication problems, inadequate follow-up, unresolved social issues, or the patient not understanding the plan. • What I control: an accurate discharge summary that reaches the GP, teach-back with the patient about medication changes and warning signs, follow-up actually booked, and a named owner for pending results. “What is the role of the multidisciplinary team?” • It is where the discharge actually happens. • Physio and OT decide whether the patient can go home, pharmacy prevents medication harm, social work solves what medicine cannot, dietitians and speech pathology handle nutrition and swallow, and nursing holds the continuous picture. • My job as RMO is to be the point of coordination, because I speak to all of them every day. Part F — Numbers to have memorised MET call criteria — Airway threat; RR under 8 or over 30; SpO2 under 90; systolic under 90; HR under 40 or over 140; sudden GCS drop of 2 or more; seizure — and “a staff member is seriously worried”. Always name that last one. GCS — Eye 4 / Verbal 5 / Motor 6. Report the breakdown, not just the total. 8 or less means secure the airway. Sepsis — Cultures before antibiotics, antibiotics within 1 hour, lactate, fluids, measure urine output. Pneumonia severity — SMART-COP or CORB (Australian), or CURB-65. Stroke — Time last known well, blood sugar, NIHSS, nil by mouth until the swallow screen. Sodium correction — No more than about 8–10 mmol/L in 24 hours. Hyperkalaemia — Stabilise (calcium) → shift (insulin and dextrose, salbutamol) → remove (binders, diuretic, dialysis). Dialysis indications — AEIOU — Acidosis, Electrolytes, Intoxication, Overload, Uraemia. Transfusion threshold — Restrictive, around 70 g/L; around 80 g/L with cardiovascular disease. Symptoms matter more than the number. AF — Stroke risk CHA2DS2-VASc, bleeding risk HAS-BLED. Cardioversion needs anticoagulation if AF has been present over 48 hours. VTE — Every inpatient gets a documented risk assessment and a prophylaxis decision. Anaphylaxis — IM adrenaline 0.5 mg of 1:1000, outer thigh, lie flat. Poisons Information Centre — 13 11 26, anywhere in Australia. Delirium screening — 4AT or CAM, plus collateral history for the baseline. NSQHS Standards — Eight standards. Standard 8 is Recognising and Responding to Acute Deterioration. Notifiable conditions — Meningococcal, measles, tuberculosis, pertussis and others — notify the state public health unit. Driving — Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive — seizure, syncope, stroke, vision, cognition. Part G — Ten sentences to learn word for word Each of these scores marks in an Australian structured interview, and each fits almost any case.
26. “First I’d want to know how sick this patient is — I’d ask for a full set of observations and the track-and-trigger score, and whether the nurse is worried.”
27. “I’d ask for help early and in parallel rather than sequentially — I’d have the nurse put out a MET call while I start my assessment.”
28. “I’d do an A to E assessment, treating each problem as I find it before moving on.”
29. “The three things I’m most concerned about and want to exclude first are…”
30. “I’d check the bedside tests first — ECG, blood glucose, a venous gas, and a pregnancy test if she’s of childbearing age.”
31. “I’d review the notes, the observation chart, the medication chart, the fluid balance, and any documented resuscitation plan or advance care directive.”
32. “I’d escalate to my registrar at this point using ISBAR, and I’d be specific about how quickly I need them.”
33. “I’d follow the local hospital protocol and Therapeutic Guidelines for the exact dosing.”
34. “I’d explain to the patient and their family what’s happening and what we’re doing, and I’d document the discussion contemporaneously.”
35. “Afterwards I’d complete an incident report if appropriate, review the patient, and make sure the pending results have a named person following them up.” And if you truly do not know: “I haven’t managed that condition before. What I would do is assess the patient with an A to E approach, make sure they’re stable, check the local protocol and Therapeutic Guidelines, and call my registrar early — because that’s exactly the situation where I shouldn’t be working it out alone.” That answer scores. Guessing does not.
